FROM:  CITY MANAGER’S OFFICE – FINANCE DIVISION

SUBJECT:  RECEIVE AND FILE THE MONTHLY INVESTMENT ACTIVITY
  REPORTS FOR AUGUST 2021.

ISSUE
Receive and file the monthly investment activity reports for August 2021.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council accept the monthly investment activity reports
for City of Palmdale and Successor Agency for August 2021.

BACKGROUND
Pursuant to Section 16 of the City of Palmdale and Successor Agency Investment
Policy, the City Treasurer shall prepare and present monthly and quarterly reports on
investments to the City Manager/Executive Director and the City Council/Directors. The
reports shall detail the type of investment, name of the issuer, purchase date, date of
maturity, amount of deposit, and rate of interest. This information shall be provided for
all City and Successor Agency pooled investments, as well as for Certificates of
Participation, Revenue Bonds, Tax Allocation Bonds, Assessment Districts and
Community Facilities District accounts which are managed by outside Fiscal Agents.

The monthly and quarterly reports provide a synopsis of the investment activity for the
City of Palmdale and Successor Agency. The reports provide information on assets,
allocations, average maturities, yields, and book valuations.

The interest rates presented are the most current rates available as of the date of this
report.

The market values presented for pooled City and Successor Agency investments are
based on closing prices for the related investment as of the date of this report. This
information was obtained from the Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg Financial Markets,
Capital Market Finances, or other reliable source of market prices.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Monthly Report on Investments
October 5, 2021
Page 2

DISCUSSION
Compliance with Investment Policy

For August, the invested portfolio amount for the City of Palmdale totaled $218,330,347,
a decrease of $17,862,406 from the previous month and $34,259,866 increase in
comparison to last year. The decrease in overall portfolio balance from the previous
month is a result of transfers out of LAIF account during the month in the amount of
$17.9 million.

The par value of Successor Agency’s portfolio as of August was $11,437,225. The
balance decreased by $1,373,575 from the prior month due to debt service payments
made during the month.

All investments meet criteria appropriate to Section 8 of the Investment Policy. The
portfolios are based on a combination of various investments, including CDs, Corporate
Notes, U.S. Treasury Securities and Government Agency Paper, each adhering to
portfolio percentage limitations.

The Finance Division is the custodian for the City and Successor Agency’s investment
portfolio and follows the three main principles of both entity’s investment policy to 1.)
Investment in financial instruments that mitigate the risk of monetary losses stemming
from market fluctuations, 2.) Establish and maintain a portfolio that has sufficient liquidity
to allow the City and Successor Agency to meet all anticipated cash requirements, and
3.) Seek out investment instruments that provide a competitive market rate of return.

Liquidity

One core approach the Finance Division focuses on, is providing liquidity to measure up
to the City and Successor Agency’s operational requirements. Thus, the Finance
Department is currently investing in two pooled funds, LAIF and CAMP. These are
intended for the daily operational activities, used for economic uncertainties and
maintenance needs. The pooled funds provide a higher liquidity ratio to ensure the City
and Successor Agency meet cash flow requirements.

Total LAIF balance for the City of Palmdale is $119,186,958 compared to July’s balance
of $137,086,958. The decrease in balance is due to the use of LAIF funds to cover debt
service and operating expenditures during the month, as well as a transfer of $17.9
million out of LAIF to be invested separately in accordance with the American Rescue
Plan Act guidance. This amount represents the first of two American Rescue Plan Act
disbursements.

Successor Agency LAIF balance at the end of August was $5,191,913, no change from
the prior month.

CAMP’s balance for City of Palmdale is $248,693, compared to July’s balance of
$248,683. The slight increase is due to interest received during the month.

The interest rates presented are the most current rates available as of the date of this
report. As of August 31, 2021, the interest rates for LAIF and CAMP investments were
at .22 percent and .05 percent, respectively. By comparison, the LAIF and CAMP
interest rates at the end of June were at .26 percent and .05 percent. Both rates have
been steadily declining. This time last year, LAIF and CAMP rates were at 0.78 percent
and 0.30, respectively.

The chart above shows both the Local Agency Investment Fund and California
Management Program’s average monthly yields from December 2020 through August
2021, the graph depicts the prolonged period of declining rates.

We anticipate a further decrease in the upcoming months, considering the economic
impacts of COVID. Overall, LAIF shows better performance than CAMP in interest rates.
The difference between the performance of the two funds is partly due to the varying
pool characteristics. CAMP’s portfolio composition is much more subject to market
volatility, resulting in performance variation.

Diversity

The Finance Division aims to diversify the investment portfolios to avoid incurring
unreasonable and avoidable risks regarding specific security types or individual financial
institutions.

City of Palmdale and Successor Agency’s investment portfolios remain strongly
diversified. The monthly reports include all investments held by both entities and current
book values as of August 31, 2021.

It is anticipated that both the City of Palmdale and Successor Agency will have sufficient
moneys to meet its expenditure requirements for the next six months as we continue to
monitor any financial impact due to the Coronavirus pandemic.

Attached are summaries of the investments on the City of Palmdale and Successor

  CODE SECTION 50050-50057

ISSUE
Adopt Resolution No. CC 2021-100, a Resolution of the City Council of the City of
Palmdale to transfer unclaimed checks from their respective funds to the general fund
pursuant to California Government Code Section 50050-50057.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council adopt Resolution No. CC 2021-100, a
Resolution of the City Council of the City of Palmdale to transfer unclaimed checks from
their respective funds to the general fund pursuant to California Government Code
Section 50050-50057.

BACKGROUND

Section 50050-50057 of the California Government Code states that “Except as
otherwise provided by law, money, excluding restitution to victims, that is not the
property of a local agency that remains unclaimed in its treasury or in the official custody
of its officers for three years is the property of the local agency after notice if not claimed
or if no verified complaint is filed and served. At any time after the expiration of the three-
year period, the treasurer of the local agency may cause a notice to be published once
a week for two successive weeks in a newspaper of general circulation published in the
local agency. At the expiration of the three-year period, money representing restitution
collected on behalf of victims shall be deposited into the Restitution Fund or used by the
local agency for purposes of victim services. allows the City to transfer for allows for the
transfer of unclaimed funds to the General Fund from other Special Funds….”
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Adopt Resolution No. CC 2021-100
October 5, 2021
Page 2

DISCUSSION

The City Treasurer desires to follow the guidelines set by California Government Code
Section 50053 and the policy set forth by this department in relation to this section.
Section 50053 states “When any such money becomes the property of a local agency
and is in a special fund, the legislative body may transfer it to the general fund.” The
total combined number of unclaimed checks for the three-year period ending June 30,
2021, is $7,969.54.

FISCAL IMPACT
The total combined number of unclaimed checks for the three-year period ending June
30, 2021, is $7,969.54. This is the maximum amount that can be transferred to the
General Fund.

STRATEGIC PLAN
Goal II: Ensure long-term fiscal health of the City and maintain funding for services.
  B. Manage resources, costs, and liabilities to ensure the City’s long-term fiscal
  health.
  C. Involve and expand engagement to enhance public oversight and
  transparency.

ISSUE
Adopt Resolution No. SA 2021-006 a Resolution of the Successor Agency to the
Community Redevelopment Agency of the City of Palmdale designating, by title and
name, those officials who are authorized to sign checks and warrants, and repealing
Resolution No. SA 2020-007.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the Successor Agency to the Community Redevelopment Agency
of the City of Palmdale adopt Resolution No. SA 2021-006 designating, by title and name,
those officials who are authorized to sign checks and warrants, and repealing Resolution
No. SA 2020-007.

BACKGROUND
Throughout the year a resolution is required whenever City-hired or City-appointed
personnel changes occur for designated, by title and name, officials who are authorized
to sign checks, drafts, warrants or other orders for the payment of money drawn in the
name of the Successor Agency to the Community Redevelopment Agency of the City of
Palmdale. The resolution is presented to the executive board members for adoption and
to also repeal the prior adopted resolution.

DISCUSSION
Resolution No. SA 2021-006 will reflect the hiring, appointment, or deletion of the

ISSUE
Approve agreement with Granicus, Inc. to continue providing government transparency
services for 3-years, in the amount of $170,367.00.

RECOMMENDATION
Approve agreement with Granicus, Inc. to continue providing government transparency
services for 3-years, in the amount of $170,367.00.

BACKGROUND
The City of Palmdale first entered into an agreement with Granicus, Inc. in November
2018 to provide agenda and meeting management, citizen participation services, and
broadcasting services for City Council and Planning Commission meetings. Since that
time, the Office of the City Clerk has been tasked with standardizing the City’s brand
recognition to reflect that of the City Council meeting agendas and staff reports, including
the various boards/commissions/standing committee agenda packets. The new
agreement would continue to provide the software capabilities to assist the City Clerk
Division maintain compliance with the California Government Code and the Ralph M.
Brown Act, as well as complete current and future tasks with efficacy.

DISCUSSION
Below is a summary of the existing key services provided by Granicus, Inc.:

    Meeting Efficiency Suite - this feature is the software tool used by the City Clerk’s
  Office to record roll call, motions, votes, and speakers during the meeting and
  helps to streamline meeting data capture and minutes production, reducing staff
  efforts and decreasing time to get minutes published.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Approval of Agreement with Granicus, Inc.

    Peak Agenda Management - This software is utilized by staff to simplify the
  agenda management and allows clerks to compile and produce agendas and
  record minutes for public meetings by creating an agenda item workflow for each
  department.

    Government Transparency Suite - this feature consists of the live in-meeting
  functions including streaming, indexing for playback, and retention of associated
  documents for playback.

    Granicus Encoding Appliance Software – This includes the LiveManager
  Software solution where webcasts are started/stopped, and agendas are amended
  and indexed.

On September 16th, AB 361 was signed into law, which will allow local government to
continue to conduct virtual meetings during a state proclaimed state of emergency.
However, the new law restricts the use of the eComment feature and ensures that the
public make real-time, in-person comments. As a result, staff had worked with Granicus
to negotiate reduced proposed rates for the remainder of the 2021/22 fiscal year, as well
as the second and third full contract years. Costs associated with Vote Cast Standard
Package have been deducted and removed from the agreement, until such time that we
are able to return to regular in-person meetings. The enclosed table is a summary of the

SUBJECT:  ADOPT RESOLUTION NO. CC 2021-101, A RESOLUTION OF THE
  CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF PALMDALE AMENDING THE
  CITY’S CLASSIFICATION AND PAY PLAN FOR GENERAL
  POSITIONS

ISSUE
Adopt Resolution No. CC 2021-101, amending the City’s Classification and Pay Plan for
General Positions.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council adopt Resolution No. CC 2021-101, amending
the City’s Classification and Pay Plan for General Positions.

BACKGROUND
The City Manager in collaboration with the Human Resources Division monitors and
evaluates positions within the organization and makes recommendations based on the
needs of the City.

DISCUSSION

Due to the increased workload and responsibilities in the City Manager’s Office there is a
need for an additional Assistant City Manager position.

The Finance Division has grown drastically over the past year and in order to address the
growing needs of the department, the increased workload, audit, and financial reporting
requirement, the division is requesting two (2) positions, a Director of Finance and a
Senior Financial Analyst.

The Director of Finance would provide the Finance Division with a strong level of
leadership, financial guidance, and expertise, and will report directly to the City Manager.
The Director of Finance assumes a leading strategic role in influencing the future of the
organization, developing policies, procedures, internal controls, segregation of duties,
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Resolution No. CC 2021-101
October 5, 2021
Page 2

and ultimately being responsible for the City’s finances and overseeing the entire Finance
Division.

The Senior Financial Analyst position is essential in ensuring that the City can meet
required deadlines, audit requirements, and ultimately maintain funding for Federal, State,
and other grant funds. Monitoring and compliance of these outside fund’s places
significant pressure on the Finance Division. It is anticipated that these pressures
continue to increase as the City continues to create new programs utilizing various
outside funding sources. Finance is currently in a position where staff members are
moving from one cycle budget to the next; and audit and financial reporting without the
positions to alleviate the workload. Staff are working extremely long hours to meet
deadlines, produce quality work, earn awards, and accomplish the highest audit opinions.
It is in the best interest of the City to provide staff with an achievable work-life balance to
ensure the long-term success of the Division.

The Neighborhood Services Department currently has a vacant Office Assistant position
that they seek to change to a Community Compliance Aide I/II position. This position will
need to be added to the Classification and Pay Plan for General positions. In the last year
there have been two (2) additional Code Enforcement Officers, one (1) Senior Code
Enforcement Officer, two (2) Community Service Officers, and two (2) full time
Neighborhood Compliance Officers added to the Community Compliance section. The
Community Compliance Aide I/II will analyze data, track activity, process warrants,
prepare reports, maintain databases, notarize documents for the Los Angeles County
Recorder and Tax Assessor’s Offices, and conduct basic follow-up field site inspections
to verify compliance.

The Economic Development Manager position is vacant. Rather than fill the position at
this level, staff is requesting a Management Analyst I. The Management Analyst I position
will assist with new business attraction, retention, and expansion efforts. This includes
responding to the overwhelming number of site proposals, parcel information, and
entitlement questions that existing staff cannot respond to in a timely manner. In addition,
the City currently has several large scale development projects that will require significant
staff time over the next two years. The Management Analyst I will serve as a project
ombudsman on these high-profile projects to ensure that various approvals are completed
on schedule.

The City Clerk Division has operated with minimal staff for quite some time due to lay-offs
that occurred in 2008 reducing the department from eight (8) full time employees to four
(4). Since the reopening of the state, the division has been inundated with a back-log of
external California Public Records Act ("CPRA") requests, claims, as well as
interdepartmental requests. The Division's workload continues to increase, without any
addition to staffing needs. The City Manager has directed the Office of the City Clerk to
assume the roles/responsibilities currently held by (10) deputized City Clerks for City
Council appointed Boards/Commissions/Committees. Additional staff is needed to meet
 Report to Mayor and City Council

October 5, 2021

the demands of each body. City Clerk is requesting a Senior Administrative Assistant to
help with the workload.

Finally, the Classification and Pay Plan for Executive staff is being consolidated with
General positions for efficiency; there is no need to have two separate documents.

ISSUE
Approve Agreement with Phoenix Group information systems for citation processing and
payment services for a term of 5 years with the amount not to exceed $600,000.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council approve Agreement No. A-7630 with Phoenix
Group Information Services for a term of 5 years with the amount not to exceed
$600,000.

BACKGROUND
The City of Palmdale has contracted with Phoenix Group Information Systems as a
software-based service to perform citation processing and payment services since 2011.
Responsibilities include data processing, correspondence processing, financial deposits
and reconciliation, adjudication processing and collections processing.
DISCUSSION
The current Agreement No. A-7630 expires on November 2, 2021, at which time the City
of Palmdale is required, through the competitive procurement process, to seek out all
qualified vendors to perform the services before they can renew the contract with Phoenix
Group. However, pursuant to City Ordinance 3.08.080, “the City’s Best Interest”
exception, staff believes that Phoenix Group services performed since 2011 have
developed more professional in nature. During this period, both City staff and Phoenix
staff have dedicated substantial time to develop and improve the procedures of
collections and services. The impact in staff time and interruption of services would be
substantial if required to transfer to another agency. Phoenix Group will honor existing
rates that were found to be the lowest responsive bid during the 2011 procurement
process. These rates will remain the same during the proposed contract term of 5 years.

ISSUE
Approve Agreement with G4S Secure Integration, LLC for the performance of a citywide
security assessment, in the amount of $183,921, for a term of two years.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Approve Agreement No. A-7658 with G4S Secure Integration, LLC. for the
  performance of a citywide security assessment, for the term of two years.
  2. Authorize the City Manager or his designee to execute Agreement No. A-7658,
  with G4S Secure Integration, LLC, including making minimal and/or non-
  substantive changes.

BACKGROUND
In response to community engagement and to ensure public safety for our residents and
staff, the City has elevated its awareness for the need to physically secure City facilities.
In May 2021, the City released a Request for Proposal (RFP) for a comprehensive
security assessment of City owned facilities, parks, and strategic areas outlined by the
City. The proposal shall protect the city’s property, assets, and citizens as well as
enhance the security for the business community at large. The selected firm would be
required to develop a complete design and install an integrated security solution, based
on the recommendations of that firm. These services and solutions are to be efficient and
economical and adhere to industry standards and best practices. The City will award a
contract to the firm whose offer represents the “best value” to the City based on
experience, price, approach, reliability of proposed solution as well as other factors
considered.

DISCUSSION
The City received ten (10) statements of qualifications and proposal packages and
reviewed each through an evaluation committee. Selection of qualified Consultants was
based upon the following scoring methodology:

  Category  Maximum Value
  Company Experience for the past 5 years  35
  Ability to perform the services  15
  Cost Proposal  20
  Technical, Plan & Scheduled Approaches  30
  TOTAL EARNED VALUE  100

The consultants were required to present their experience in providing services for
government, institutions, and corporations, demonstrate records of providing high quality
and timely delivery of goods and services and provide a well-established documented
and effective quality control program. The consultants were also required to have the
capacity to handle assigned projects in a timely manner, provide qualifications of project
team members who will be assigned to the contract, and demonstrate coordination of
work with subcontractors and customers for minimum interference. The following firms
submitted statements of qualifications and proposal packages.

  Name of Proposer  Location
  1. G4S Secure  Los Angeles, CA
  2. Blue Violet  Fountain Valley, CA
  3. Vector Resources  Torrance, CA
  4. Johnson Controls  Glendale, WI
  5. ADT  Boca Raton, FL
  6. Burns & McDonnell  Kansas City, MO
  7. RD Systems  Minneapolis, MN
  8. Sierra Group  Pennsylvania, PA
  9. TRC  Windsor, CO
  10. Vantage  New York, NY

The evaluation committee identified four (4) firms with exceptional qualifications; G4S
Secure, Blue Violet, Vector Resources and Johnson Controls and invited all four firms to
participate in an interview for final consultant selection. After the interviews concluded,
the evaluation committee determined that G4S Secure Integration was the most qualified
consultant to perform the requested services based on their comprehensive project
approach and prior experience with facilities of similar scope and size.

Following award of agreement, G4S Secure Integration, LLC will develop a
Comprehensive Security Risk Assessment Report (CSRAR) that will include:
   Executive summary;

ISSUE
Approve Consultant Service Agreement with Schneider Electric in the amount of
$95,000, for a term of one (1) year with an option to extend an additional year, in
association with energy service contractor services for the City’s proposed energy
efficiency projects.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Approve Consultant Service Agreement with Schneider Electric in the amount of
  $95,000, for a term of one (1) year with an option to extend an additional year, in
  association with energy service contractor services for the City’s proposed
  energy efficiency projects; and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager, or his designee, to execute Agreement No. A-7640
  with Schneider Electric, including making minor and non-substantive changes.

BACKGROUND
In its ongoing efforts to improve energy efficiency and reduce City energy costs, staff has
been working to identify and implement energy efficiency projects through audit, design,
and construction management support. In May 2021, the City solicited Requests for
Qualifications and Experience (RFQ&Es) from energy services companies (ESCO’s)
through an open consultant selection process. The ESCO’s were to be capable of
designing and implementing energy conservation, energy efficiency, energy generation
and other energy related capital improvement services (“Projects”) pursuant to California
Government Code Section 4217.10 et seq. The projects would require no upfront capital
 Report to Mayor and City Council

from the City and would pay for themselves from energy and operational savings within
the useful life. The projects would continue to reduce energy costs to the City once paid
for. The required Scope of Services included, conducting an investment grade audit of
City facilities energy use and to provide a comprehensive report of its findings and
recommendations. Upon review and assessment of this report, staff will return with
recommended projects for execution by Schneider through an Energy Project
Performance Contract.

DISCUSSION
The City received three (3) qualification packages, and upon review by an evaluation
committee and interview of the top two candidates, staff has selected Schneider Electric
as the most qualified firm.

The consultants were required to present their experience in providing services for

and timely delivery of goods and services and provide a well-established documented
and effective quality control program. The consultants were also required to have the
capacity to handle assigned projects in a timely manner, provide qualifications of project
team members who will be assigned to the contract, and demonstrate coordination of
work with subcontractors and customers for minimum interference. The resulting scores

R/W Acquisition: OPC’s approach is summarized as follows:

Pre-Planning: The R/W approach begins with early planning, diligent
communication and reporting, and established processes that are instrumental to
keeping the projects on-time and within budget. The most important element of
our approach will be to meet with the City staff and the project design consultant
early to determine the project requirements and objectives, and establish
approved forms/documents to be used and approval processes for the City’s R/W
program. Additionally, factors impacting appraisal decisions will be clarified;
determining type of interests to be acquired, i.e. fee, easement, and length of
Temporary Construction Easements (TCE). After meeting with the City/design
engineer, OPC will prepare a revised R/W delivery schedule and parcel matrix of
R/W impacts incorporating all pertinent information for distribution.

Pre-Acquisition: OPC will secure preliminary title reports from Commonwealth
Land Title Insurance Company to identify existing easements/adverse title
conditions for all impacted properties. Should adverse title conditions exist, OPC
shall meet with the Project Team City to determine an appropriate correctional
plan to address prior to commencement of negotiations.

Appraisal: As the appraiser is oftentimes the first point of contact with a property
owner, we strive to build a relationship with the property owner that will facilitate
a smooth transition to the agent so that when the offer is presented, the property
owner has a level of comfort and confidence with OPC’s right of way service
professionals. After sending a certified letter to the owner of Notice of Decision
to Appraise inviting the owner to accompany the appraiser during the inspection
and requesting information concerning history and input for the property, the
appraiser will prepare a narrative appraisal report that conforms to the Uniform
Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice (USPAP). The appraisal study and
report are intended to serve as an acquisition appraisal and will be prepared in a
summary format consistent with the specifications for narrative appraisal reports.

Negotiation: Upon receipt of the appraisal, a draft offer package and applicable
right of way agreements/documentation will be submitted to the City for approval.
Following the City Council’s approval of just compensation, OPC will present the
City’s written purchase offer to the owner and/or owner’s representative.
Negotiations will involve an interactive, face-to-face discussion with the property
owner about his/her property; explanation of the project and its impacts to the
property; explanation of the appraisal process and how the value was concluded;
and answer any questions or concerns the owners may have. All of our agents
are licensed with the California Bureau of Real Estate (BRE) and trained to utilize
a non-coercive, integrative negotiation style to overcome all hurdles in reaching a
settlement in the most efficient manner possible. Our agents will negotiate in
good faith, with an open mind for creative solutions that will be mutually
beneficial to all parties involved.

Supplemental negotiations may also include addressing any objection or
question concerning the project the owner has by conferring with the City. Once
an agreement is reached, OPC will submit the appropriate executed documents to
the City for approval. Upon the City’s approval of the appropriate documents,
escrow will be opened by submitting an instruction letter providing the purchase
contract, title insurance coverage, and notarized Deed to escrow agent. OPC will
assist with any due diligence requirements and resolve adverse title conditions
preceding the close of escrow and will coordinate payment of just compensation.
The City will be furnished with copies of the recorded Deeds and title insurance
policies following the close of escrow.

Fiber Optic Infrastructure Planning: Fiber optic interconnect planning will include
confirmation of existing fiber tie-in locations and determination of the preferred
side of street based on presence of existing sidewalk (conduit installed beneath
sidewalk is better protected; location of signal cabinets (to minimize cost of
lateral conduit runs); presence of utilities and potential for conflicts; and future
widening projects (we will try to avoid conduit in areas that are not fully built out).
Once a preliminary route is established, we will obtain clearance requirements
from utility owners and conduct a field review to identify utility conflicts on the
preferred side of street. Most utilities conflicts can be easily addressed in the
field by the boring contractor and do not require design phase potholing.
Potential problems can occur when there are too many utilities in the parkway, or
there are high risk utilities such as Palmdale water mains and SoCal Gas
transmission lines that require as much as 10’ clearance. Fiber infrastructure
routing will be finalized following receipt of pothole information and submitted to
the City for approval. The following outlines our initial approach for each street.

Avenue S from 55th Street East to 60th Street East: Under Phase II of the North
County ITS Project (designed by TES), 2-3” conduits and 72 single mode fiber
optic cable was installed on the south side of Avenue S to a N48E pull box
adjacent to the traffic signal cabinet at Avenue S/55th Street East. Since sidewalk
is also built out on the south side between 55th Street East and 60th Street East
(except for the parcel at 60th Street East), we will focus on extending the conduit
on the south side.

Avenue R from 40th Street East to 70th Street East: This conduit run is much
longer than Avenue S and involves existing traffic signal cabinets at 55th Street
East (SE corner) and 60th Street East (SE corner). The traffic signal cabinet at
40th Street East (tie-in location) is on the NE corner which suggests the existing
fiber trunk may also be on the north side. In addition, the new conduit will need
to cross 47th Street East (Caltrans R/W), and pick up new cabinets at 65th Street
East and 70th Street East. If installation of new traffic signal cabinets on the
south side is acceptable to the City, then we will focus on the south side between
55th Street East and 70th Street East. If the existing trunk fiber is on the north
side at 40th Street East, then we would determine an appropriate location to
cross from the north side to the south side based on utility conflicts and other
factors.

Design Phase Potholing: Potholing during the design phase can be beneficial to
identifying and resolving underground utility conflicts along the fiber optic
conduit route and at new traffic signal pole locations where position impacts the

Topographic Survey:

Avenue R: 40th Street East to 70th Street East. A full aerial topographic survey
and a ground survey will be obtained for the entire R/W (existing and proposed)
for the project limits along Avenue R from 40th St East to 70th St East. The
survey will obtain all visible surface culture, including curb, gutter, sidewalk,
trees, driveways, existing striping, above ground utilities, etc. A ground survey
will be utilized to obtain horizontal, vertical control and R/W will be taken at
minimum 100’ intervals. The ground survey will also pick up features missed by
the aerial survey.

New Traffic Signal Intersections. A ground survey will be obtained at the new
traffic signal intersections, with 50’ intervals taken for at least 450’ on each
approach. Additional 50’ intervals will be taken as needed (plus an additional
100’) based on our project approach for each intersection where widening is

back of walk, and R/W at BCR, ECR, and half delta, and at all critical locations on
the existing ramps needed to determine existing slope for path of wheelchair,
side slope at the curb, approach slope on the street, and drainage.

Horizontal and vertical control will be based on the California Coordinate System
NAD 83 and vertical NAVD 1988. Survey data will be imported into AutoCAD,
reviewed for completeness and the base mapping will be prepared. The base

ISSUE
Approve Supplemental Agreement No. 2with Manhole Adjusting, Inc. in association with
PN 806, 2021 Local Streets Cape Seal Project, in the amount of $1,046,773.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Approve Supplemental Agreement No. 2 to Agreement No. A-7505 for PN 806,
  2021 Local Streets Cape Seal Project, in the amount of $1,046,773.
  2. Authorize the City Manager or his designee to execute Supplemental Agreement
  No. 2 to Agreement No. A-7505, with Manhole Adjusting, Inc., including making
  minimal and/or non-substantive changes.

BACKGROUND
Project No. 806, the 2021 Local Street Cape Seal Project, provides for resurfacing of
approximately 2.525 million square feet of local streets throughout the City with a System
1 ARAM cape seal treatment. This project was awarded to Manhole Adjusting, Inc. in
June 2021 and construction has commenced with approximately 70% complete.
Supplemental Agreement No. 1 provided for installation of a leveling course along a
section of the original streets and surface preparation of additional streets prior to the
cape seal installation.

DISCUSSION

In response to complaints received from concerned residents, City staff reviewed and
assessed the condition of additional streets to receive a cape seal treatment and to
potentially be included in Project No. 806. The additional local streets are residential and
collector streets located north of Avenue S between Parkland Dr. and The Groves. The
Contractor submitted a proposal for System 1 ARAM cape seal installation, in accordance
with the contract documents, and agreed to perform the extra work at the original bid unit
prices without markup if remobilizations were not required. The initial project scope was
completed sooner than anticipated and therefore time is available to complete the
 Report to Mayor and City Council

additional streets before cold weather sets in. It is beneficial to the City to resurface these
local streets now as budget for street resurfacing is available. In addition, with
construction material and labor costs continually increasing, waiting until the next
resurfacing season would result in a higher cost to the City.

The total additional square footage of resurfacing is 1,181,445. Supplemental Agreement
No. 2 provides for additional traffic control, remaining surface preparation, cape seal
installation, striping replacement, and utility adjustment on the added streets.

ISSUE
Adopt Resolution No. CC 2020-096, a Resolution of the City Council of the City of
Palmdale declaring results of majority protest proceedings and establishing the
Palmdale Tourism Improvement District (PTID).

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:

  1. Hold a public meeting and receive public comments on the formation of the PTID;

  2. Adopt Resolution No. CC 2021-096, a Resolution of the City Council of the City
  of Palmdale declaring results of majority protest proceedings and establishing the
  PTID; and,

  3. Authorize the City Manager or his designee to execute any actions related to the
  establishment of the PTID.

BACKGROUND
As outlined in the Property and Business Improvement Law of 1994, Streets and
Highways Code § 36600 et seq. (94 Law), which allows a City to form a Tourism
Improvement District (TID), the City of Palmdale, as part of the PTID formation process,
carried out the following:

August 17, 2021  RESOLUTION OF INTENTION HEARING
  The City Council approved the Resolution of Intention No. CC
  2021-070 to establish the PTID. The City Council received a public
  comment in support of the PTID.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Palmdale Tourism Improvement District
October 5, 2021
Page 2

August 18, 2021  NOTICE MAILED TO OWNERS
  The 94 Law requires the City to mail written notice to the owners of
  all businesses proposed to be within the PTID. Mailing the notice
  begins a mandatory forty-five (45) day period in which owners may
  protest PTID formation. City staff mailed the notice, a copy of the
  approved resolution, and a draft of the Management District Plan.

September 7, 2021 PUBLIC HEARING
  The City held a Public Hearing to allowed public testimony on the
  formation of the PTID and levy of assessments. No actions were
  required at the council meeting. The City Council received multiple
  public comments in support of the PTID.

October 5, 2021  FINAL PUBLIC HEARING
  The City Council will hold a public meeting and receive public
  comments on the formation of the PTID. If the Council, following the
  public hearing, decides to establish the PTID, the Council shall adopt
  a resolution of formation.

As of the writing of this staff report, the City has not received comments against the
formation of the proposed PTID.

The proposed PTID would be a partnership between the City and the hotels in Palmdale
to create additional tourism and visitor opportunities that both visitors and residents can
enjoy. The benefits a TID can come in a variety of forms such as signature events,
enhancing the current tourism attractions, development of additional destinations and
infrastructure improvements. This increase in tourism and business travel would positively
impact hotels, restaurants, and local small businesses.

DISCUSSION
The hotel owners and managers in Palmdale are proposing to form the PTID for a five-
year term. The proposed services include sales, marketing and communication
programs, destination development and promotion of special events. All services
provided by the PTID are intended to attract new visitors and increase demand for
overnight visitation to assessed businesses. All services provided by the PTID are
intended to attract new and weekend visitation when hotels experience lower
occupancy. If established, the PTID would generate approximately $900,000 annually.

The Management District Plan (Attachment 1) includes the proposed boundary of the
proposed PTID, a service plan and budget, and governance. The PTID will include all
current and future lodging businesses within the boundaries of Palmdale. The City met
with representatives of several of the Palmdale lodging businesses to discuss and review
the proposed Management District Plan.

Re: Palmdale Tourism Improvement District
October 5, 2021
Page 3

As proposed, the PTID is expected to have a five-year term, beginning November 1, 2021
through October 31, 2026. The self-assessment will be implemented beginning
November 1, 2021. Once per year, beginning on the anniversary of the TID formation,
there is a 30-day period in which business owners paying 50% or more of the total self-
assessment may protest and begin proceedings to terminate the TID.

The annual self-assessment rate is two percent of gross short-term room rental revenue.
Based on the benefit received, assessments will not be collected on stays of more than
30 consecutive days; stays of any officer or employee of a foreign government who is
exempt by reason of express provision of federal law or international treaty; and stays
pursuant to contracts executed prior to November 1, 2021.

The City will collect the self-assessment from each lodging business located within the
PTID boundaries and distribute the assessment to Visit Palmdale. Visit Palmdale will have
the responsibility of managing TID programs as provided in the Management District Plan.
The PTID shall pay the City a fee equal to one percent of the amount of assessment
collected to cover the costs of collection and administration.

The proposed PTID program includes regional marketing efforts. These efforts would
allow the PTID to collaborate on joint tourism and marketing opportunities with the
County of Los Angeles and City of Lancaster to enhance tourism throughout the
Antelope Valley. Regional marketing efforts would benefit business, hotels, and
entertainment venues throughout the Antelope Valley.

FISCAL IMPACT
If the PTID is approved, the City would receive a fee of one percent of the total amount
collected to cover the costs of administration. In addition, there may be an increase in
transient occupancy tax and sales tax revenues as PTID programs are intended to
increase visitation to the City.

  I.  OVERVIEW
Developed by local hoteliers and the City of Palmdale (City), the Palmdale Tourism Improvement
District (PTID) is an assessment district proposed to provide specific benefits to payors, by funding
marketing and sales promotion efforts for assessed businesses. This approach has been used
successfully in other destination areas throughout the country to provide the benefit of additional
room night sales directly to payors.

Location:  The PTID includes all lodging businesses, existing and in the future, available for
  public occupancy located within the boundaries of the City of Palmdale, as shown on
  the map in Section III.

Services:  The PTID is designed to provide specific benefits directly to payors by increasing
  awareness and demand for room night sales. Sales, marketing & communications and
  destination development programs will increase demand for overnight tourism and
  market payors as tourist, meeting and event destinations, thereby increasing demand
  for room night sales.

Budget:  The total PTID annual assessment budget for the initial year of its five (5) year
  operation is anticipated to be approximately $900,000. A similar budget is expected to
  apply to subsequent years, but this budget is expected to fluctuate as room sales do.

Cost:  The annual assessment rate is two percent (2%) of gross short-term room rental
  revenue. Based on the benefit received, assessments will not be collected on: stays of
  more than thirty (30) consecutive days; stays of any officer or employee of a foreign
  government who is exempt by reason of express provision of federal law or
  international treaty; and stays pursuant to contracts executed prior to November 1,
  2021.

Collection:  The City shall be responsible for collecting the assessment on a monthly basis
  (including any delinquencies, penalties and interest) from each lodging business
  located in the boundaries of the PTID. The City shall take all reasonable efforts to
  collect the assessments from each lodging business.

Duration:  The PTID will have a five (5) year life, beginning November 1, 2021 through October
  31, 2026. Once per year, beginning on the anniversary of PTID formation, there is a
  thirty (30) day period in which owners paying fifty percent (50%) or more of the
  assessment may protest and initiate a City Council hearing on PTID termination.

Management: Visit Palmdale (VP) will serve as the PTID’s Owners’ Association. The Owners’
  Association is charged with managing funds and implementing programs in
  accordance with this Plan, and must provide annual reports to the City Council.

 II.  BACKGROUND
TIDs are an evolution of the traditional Business Improvement District. The first TID was formed
in West Hollywood, California in 1989. Since then, over 100 California destinations have followed
suit. In recent years, other states have begun adopting the California model – Montana, South Dakota,
Washington, Colorado, Texas and Louisiana have adopted TID laws. Several other states are in the
process of adopting their own legislation. The cities of Wichita, Kansas and Newark, New Jersey used
an existing business improvement district law to form a TID. And, some cities, like Portland, Oregon
and Memphis, Tennessee have utilized their home rule powers to create TIDs without a state law.

the market-based promotion of tourism districts. TIDs allow lodging business owners to organize
their efforts to increase demand for room night sales. Lodging business owners within the TID pay
an assessment and those funds are used to provide services that increase demand for room night sales.

In California, most TIDs are formed pursuant to the Property and Business Improvement District
Law of 1994. This law allows for the creation of a benefit assessment district to raise funds within a
specific geographic area. The key difference between TIDs and other benefit assessment districts is that funds raised
are returned to the private non-profit corporation governing the district.

There are many benefits to TIDs:

 Funds must be spent on services and improvements that provide a specific benefit only to those
  who pay;
 Funds cannot be diverted to general government programs;
 They are customized to fit the needs of payors in each destination;
 They allow for a wide range of services;
 They are designed, created and governed by those who will pay the assessment; and
 They provide a stable, long-term funding source for tourism promotion.

The PTID assessment is not a property-based assessment subject to the requirements of Proposition
218. Courts have found Proposition 218 limited the term ‘assessments’ to levies on real property.1
Rather, the PTID assessment is a business-based assessment, and is subject to Proposition 26.
Pursuant to Proposition 26 all levies are a tax unless they fit one of seven exceptions. Two of these
exceptions apply to the PTID, a “specific benefit” and a “specific government service.” Both require
that the costs of benefits or services do not exceed the reasonable costs to the City of conferring the
benefits or providing the services.

  1. Specific Benefit
Proposition 26 requires that assessment funds be expended on, “a specific benefit conferred or
privilege granted directly to the payor that is not provided to those not charged, and which does not

 exceed the reasonable costs to the local government of conferring the benefit or granting the
privilege.”2 The services in this Plan are designed to provide targeted benefits directly to assessed
businesses, and are intended only to provide benefits and services directly to those businesses paying
the assessment. These services are tailored not to serve the general public, businesses in general, or
parcels of land, but rather to serve the specific businesses within the PTID. The activities described
in this Plan are specifically targeted to increase demand for room night sales for assessed lodging
businesses within the boundaries of the PTID, and are narrowly tailored. PTID funds will be used
exclusively to provide the specific benefit of increased demand for room night sales directly to the
assessees. Assessment funds shall not be used to feature non-assessed lodging businesses in PTID
programs, or to directly generate sales for non-assessed businesses. The activities paid for from
assessment revenues are business services constituting and providing specific benefits to the assessed
businesses.

The assessment imposed by this PTID is for a specific benefit conferred directly to the payors that is
not provided to those not charged. The specific benefit conferred directly to the payors is an increase
in demand for room night sales. The specific benefit of an increase in demand for room night sales
for assessed lodging businesses will be provided only to lodging businesses paying the district
assessment, with marketing and sales programs promoting lodging businesses paying the PTID
assessment. The marketing, sales & communications and destination development programs will be
designed to increase room night sales at each assessed lodging businesses. Because they are necessary
to provide the marketing, sales & communications and destination development programs that
specifically benefit the assessed lodging businesses, the administration and contingency services also
provide the specific benefit of increased demand for room night sales to the assessed lodging
businesses.

Although the PTID, in providing specific benefits to payors, may produce incidental benefits to non-
paying businesses, the incidental benefit does not preclude the services from being considered a
specific benefit. The legislature has found that, “A specific benefit is not excluded from classification
as a ‘specific benefit’ merely because an indirect benefit to a nonpayor occurs incidentally and without
cost to the payor as a consequence of providing the specific benefit to the payor.”3

  2. Specific Government Service
The assessment may also be utilized to provide, “a specific government service or product provided
directly to the payor that is not provided to those not charged, and which does not exceed the
reasonable costs to the local government of providing the service or product.”4 The legislature has
recognized that marketing and promotions services like those to be provided by the PTID are
government services within the meaning of Proposition 265. Further, the legislature has determined
that “a specific government service is not excluded from classification as a ‘specific government
service’ merely because an indirect benefit to a nonpayor occurs incidentally and without cost to the
payor as a consequence of providing the specific government service to the payor.”6

  3. Reasonable Cost
PTID services will be implemented carefully to ensure they do not exceed the reasonable cost of such
services. The full amount assessed will be used to provide the services described herein. Funds will

The PTID-funded programs are all targeted directly at and feature only assessed businesses. It is,

  D. Assessment
The annual assessment rate is two percent (2%) of gross short term room rental revenue. Based on
the benefit received, assessments will not be collected on: stays of more than thirty (30) consecutive
days; stays of any officer or employee of a foreign government who is exempt by reason of express
provision of federal law or international treaty; and stays pursuant to contracts executed prior to
November 1, 2021.

The term “gross room rental revenue” as used herein means: the consideration charged, whether or
not received, for the occupancy of space in a hotel, valued in money, whether to be received in money,
goods, labor or otherwise, including all receipts, cash credits and property and services of any kind or
nature, without any deduction therefrom whatsoever. Gross room rental revenue shall not include any
federal, state or local taxes collected, including but not limited to transient occupancy taxes.

The assessment is levied upon and a direct obligation of the assessed lodging business. However, the
assessed lodging business may, at its discretion, pass the assessment on to transients. The amount of
assessment, if passed on to each transient, shall be disclosed in advance and separately stated from the
amount of rent charged and any other applicable taxes, and each transient shall receive a receipt for
payment from the business. If the PTID assessment is identified separately it shall be disclosed as the
“PTID Assessment.” As an alternative, the disclosure may include the amount of the PTID
assessment and the amount of the assessment imposed pursuant to the California Tourism Marketing
Act, Government Code §13995 et seq. and shall be disclosed as the “Tourism Assessment.” The
assessment is imposed solely upon, and is the sole obligation of the assessed lodging business even if
it is passed on to transients. The assessment shall not be considered revenue for any purpose, including
calculation of transient occupancy taxes.

Bonds shall not be issued.

  E. Penalties and Interest
The PTID shall reimburse the City of Palmdale for any costs associated with collecting unpaid
assessments. If sums in excess of the delinquent PTID assessment are sought to be recovered in the
same collection action by the City, the PTID shall bear its pro rata share of such collection costs.
Assessed businesses which are delinquent in paying the assessment shall be responsible for paying:
  1. Original Delinquency: Any lodging business owner who fails to remit any assessment imposed
  by this section within the time required shall pay a penalty of 10 percent (10%) of the amount
  of the unpaid assessment in addition to the amount of the assessment.

  3. Fraud: If the City determines that the nonpayment of any remittance due under this section is

  5. Penalties Merged with Assessment: Every penalty imposed and such interest as accrues under the

  F. Time and Manner for Collecting Assessments
The PTID assessment will be implemented beginning November 1, 2021 and will continue for five (5)
years through October 31, 2026. The City will be responsible for collecting the assessment on a
monthly basis (including any delinquencies, penalties and interest) from each lodging business. The
City shall take all reasonable efforts to collect the assessments from each lodging business. The City
shall forward the assessments collected to the Owners’ Association.

  V.  GOVERNANCE

  A. Owners’ Association
The City Council, through adoption of this Management District Plan, has the right, pursuant to
Streets and Highways Code §36651, to identify the body that shall implement the proposed program,
which shall be the Owners’ Association of the PTID as defined in Streets and Highways Code §36612.
The City Council has determined that the to-be-formed nonprofit corporation, Visit Palmdale (VP),
will serve as the Owners’ Association for the PTID.

VP shall be comprised of five (5) to seven (7) directors, in which a majority of the directors shall be
owners or owner representatives of businesses paying the PTID assessment. The Board will also
include representation from the City and may include businesses with an interest in tourism. VP shall
have full authority to manage matters related to the PTID including, but not limited to, management
of assessment funds and full decision-making authority regarding PTID programs in accordance with
this Plan.

  B. Brown Act and California Public Records Act Compliance
An Owners’ Association is a private entity and may not be considered a public entity for any purpose,
nor may its board members or staff be considered to be public officials for any purpose. The Owners’
Association is, however, subject to government regulations relating to transparency, namely the Ralph
M. Brown Act and the California Public Records Act. These regulations are designed to promote
public accountability. The Owners’ Association acts as a legislative body under the Ralph M. Brown
Act (Government Code §54950 et seq.). Thus, meetings of the VP board and certain committees
must be held in compliance with the public notice and other requirements of the Brown Act. The
Owners’ Association is also subject to the record keeping and disclosure requirements of the California
Public Records Act. Accordingly, the Owners’ Association shall publicly report any action taken and
the vote or abstention on that action of each member present for the action.

  C. Annual Report
VP shall present an annual report at the end of each year of operation to the City Council pursuant to
Streets and Highways Code §36650 (see Appendix 1). The annual report shall include:
   Any proposed changes in the boundaries of the improvement district or in any benefit zones
  or classification of businesses within the district.
   The improvements and activities to be provided for that fiscal year.
   An estimate of the cost of providing the improvements and the activities for that fiscal year.
   The method and basis of levying the assessment in sufficient detail to allow each business
  owner to estimate the amount of the assessment to be levied against his or her business for
  that fiscal year.
   The estimated amount of any surplus or deficit revenues to be carried over from a previous
  fiscal year.
   The estimated amount of any contributions to be made from sources other than assessments
  levied pursuant to this part.

  ARTICLE 1. Declarations

36600. Citation of part

This part shall be known and may be cited as the “Property and Business Improvement District Law of 1994.”

36601. Legislative findings and declarations; Legislative guidance

The Legislature finds and declares all of the following:
  (a) Businesses located and operating within business districts in some of this state’s communities are
  economically disadvantaged, are underutilized, and are unable to attract customers due to inadequate
  facilities, services, and activities in the business districts.
  (b) It is in the public interest to promote the economic revitalization and physical maintenance of business
  districts in order to create jobs, attract new businesses, and prevent the erosion of the business districts.
  (c) It is of particular local benefit to allow business districts to fund business related improvements,
  maintenance, and activities through the levy of assessments upon the businesses or real property that receive
  benefits from those improvements.
  (d) Assessments levied for the purpose of conferring special benefit upon the real property or a specific
  benefit upon the businesses in a business district are not taxes for the general benefit of a city, even if property,
  businesses, or persons not assessed receive incidental or collateral effects that benefit them.
  (e) Property and business improvement districts formed throughout this state have conferred special benefits
  upon properties and businesses within their districts and have made those properties and businesses more
  useful by providing the following benefits:
  (1) Crime reduction. A study by the Rand Corporation has confirmed a 12-percent reduction in the
  incidence of robbery and an 8-percent reduction in the total incidence of violent crimes within the
  30 districts studied.
  (2) Job creation.
  (3) Business attraction.
  (4) Business retention.
  (5) Economic growth.
  (6) New investments.
  (f) With the dissolution of redevelopment agencies throughout the state, property and business improvement
  districts have become even more important tools with which communities can combat blight, promote
  economic opportunities, and create a clean and safe environment.
  (g) Since the enactment of this act, the people of California have adopted Proposition 218, which added
  Article XIII D to the Constitution in order to place certain requirements and restrictions on the formation of,
  and activities, expenditures, and assessments by property-based districts. Article XIII D of the Constitution
  provides that property-based districts may only levy assessments for special benefits.
  (h) The act amending this section is intended to provide the Legislature’s guidance with regard to this act, its
  interaction with the provisions of Article XIII D of the Constitution, and the determination of special benefits
  in property-based districts.
  (1) The lack of legislative guidance has resulted in uncertainty and inconsistent application of this
  act, which discourages the use of assessments to fund needed improvements, maintenance, and
  activities in property-based districts, contributing to blight and other underutilization of property.
  (2) Activities undertaken for the purpose of conferring special benefits upon property to be assessed
  inherently produce incidental or collateral effects that benefit property or persons not assessed.
  Therefore, for special benefits to exist as a separate and distinct category from general benefits, the
PTID Management District Plan  13

   incidental or collateral effects of those special benefits are inherently part of those special benefits.
  The mere fact that special benefits produce incidental or collateral effects that benefit property or
  persons not assessed does not convert any portion of those special benefits or their incidental or
  collateral effects into general benefits.
  (3) It is of the utmost importance that property-based districts created under this act have clarity
  regarding restrictions on assessments they may levy and the proper determination of special benefits.
  Legislative clarity with regard to this act will provide districts with clear instructions and courts with
  legislative intent regarding restrictions on property-based assessments, and the manner in which
  special benefits should be determined.

36602. Purpose of part

The purpose of this part is to supplement previously enacted provisions of law that authorize cities to levy assessments
within property and business improvement districts, to ensure that those assessments conform to all constitutional
requirements and are determined and assessed in accordance with the guidance set forth in this act. This part does not
affect or limit any other provisions of law authorizing or providing for the furnishing of improvements or activities or
the raising of revenue for these purposes.

36603. Preemption of authority or charter city to adopt ordinances levying assessments

Nothing in this part is intended to preempt the authority of a charter city to adopt ordinances providing for a different
method of levying assessments for similar or additional purposes from those set forth in this part. A property and
business improvement district created pursuant to this part is expressly exempt from the provisions of the Special
Assessment Investigation, Limitation and Majority Protest Act of 1931 (Division 4 (commencing with Section 2800)).

36603.5. Part prevails over conflicting provisions

Any provision of this part that conflicts with any other provision of law shall prevail over the other provision of law,
as to districts created under this part.

36604. Severability

This part is intended to be construed liberally and, if any provision is held invalid, the remaining provisions shall
remain in full force and effect. Assessments levied under this part are not special taxes.

36624. Changes to proposed assessments

At the conclusion of the public hearing to establish the district, the city council may adopt, revise, change, reduce, or
modify the proposed assessment or the type or types of improvements, maintenance, and activities to be funded with
the revenues from the assessments. Proposed assessments may only be revised by reducing any or all of them. At the
public hearing, the city council may only make changes in, to, or from the boundaries of the proposed property and
business improvement district that will exclude territory that will not benefit from the proposed improvements,
maintenance, and activities. Any modifications, revisions, reductions, or changes to the proposed assessment district
shall be reflected in the notice and map recorded pursuant to Section 36627.

36625. Resolution of formation

  (a) If the city council, following the public hearing, decides to establish a proposed property and business
  improvement district, the city council shall adopt a resolution of formation that shall include, but is not limited
  to, all of the following:
  (1) A brief description of the proposed improvements, maintenance, and activities, the amount of
  the proposed assessment, a statement as to whether the assessment will be levied on property,
  businesses, or both within the district, a statement on whether bonds will be issued, and a description
  of the exterior boundaries of the proposed district, which may be made by reference to any plan or
  map that is on file with the clerk. The descriptions and statements need not be detailed and shall be
  sufficient if they enable an owner to generally identify the nature and extent of the improvements,
  maintenance, and activities and the location and extent of the proposed district.
  (2) The number, date of adoption, and title of the resolution of intention.
  (3) The time and place where the public hearing was held concerning the establishment of the
  district.
  (4) A determination regarding any protests received. The city shall not establish the district or levy
  assessments if a majority protest was received.
  (5) A statement that the properties, businesses, or properties and businesses in the district established
  by the resolution shall be subject to any amendments to this part.
  (6) A statement that the improvements, maintenance, and activities to be conferred on businesses
  and properties in the district will be funded by the levy of the assessments. The revenue from the
  levy of assessments within a district shall not be used to provide improvements, maintenance, or
  activities outside the district or for any purpose other than the purposes specified in the resolution
  of intention, as modified by the city council at the hearing concerning establishment of the district.
  Notwithstanding the foregoing, improvements and activities that must be provided outside the
  district boundaries to create a special or specific benefit to the assessed parcels or businesses may
  be provided, but shall be limited to marketing or signage pointing to the district.
  (7) A finding that the property or businesses within the area of the property and business
  improvement district will be benefited by the improvements, maintenance, and activities funded by
  the proposed assessments, and, for a property-based district, that property within the district will
  receive a special benefit.
  (8) In a property-based district, the total amount of all special benefits to be conferred on the
  properties within the property-based district.
  (b) The adoption of the resolution of formation and, if required, recordation of the notice and map pursuant
  to Section 36627 shall constitute the levy of an assessment in each of the fiscal years referred to in the
  management district plan.

 36627. Notice and assessment diagram

Following adoption of the resolution establishing district assessments on properties pursuant to Section 36625, the
clerk shall record a notice and an assessment diagram pursuant to Section 3114. No other provision of Division 4.5
(commencing with Section 3100) applies to an assessment district created pursuant to this part.

36628. Establishment of separate benefit zones within district; Categories of businesses

The city council may establish one or more separate benefit zones within the district based upon the degree of benefit
derived from the improvements or activities to be provided within the benefit zone and may impose a different
assessment within each benefit zone. If the assessment is to be levied on businesses, the city council may also define
categories of businesses based upon the degree of benefit that each will derive from the improvements or activities to
be provided within the district and may impose a different assessment or rate of assessment on each category of
business, or on each category of business within each zone.

36628.5. Assessments on businesses or property owners

The city council may levy assessments on businesses or on property owners, or a combination of the two, pursuant to
this part. The city council shall structure the assessments in whatever manner it determines corresponds with the
distribution of benefits from the proposed improvements, maintenance, and activities, provided that any property-
based assessment conforms with the requirements set forth in paragraph (2) of subdivision (k) of Section 36622.

36629. Provisions and procedures applicable to benefit zones and business categories

All provisions of this part applicable to the establishment, modification, or disestablishment of a property and business
improvement district apply to the establishment, modification, or disestablishment of benefit zones or categories of
business. The city council shall, to establish, modify, or disestablish a benefit zone or category of business, follow the
procedure to establish, modify, or disestablish a property and business improvement district.

36630. Expiration of district; Creation of new district

If a property and business improvement district expires due to the time limit set pursuant to subdivision (h) of Section
36622, a new management district plan may be created and the district may be renewed pursuant to this part.

  CHAPTER 3. Assessments

36631. Time and manner of collection of assessments; Delinquent payments

The collection of the assessments levied pursuant to this part shall be made at the time and in the manner set forth by
the city council in the resolution levying the assessment. Assessments levied on real property may be collected at the
same time and in the same manner as for the ad valorem property tax, and may provide for the same lien priority and
penalties for delinquent payment. All delinquent payments for assessments levied pursuant to this part may be charged
interest and penalties.
36632. Assessments to be based on estimated benefit; Classification of real property and businesses; Exclusion
of residential and agricultural property

  (a) The assessments levied on real property pursuant to this part shall be levied on the basis of the estimated
  benefit to the real property within the property and business improvement district. The city council may
  classify properties for purposes of determining the benefit to property of the improvements and activities
  provided pursuant to this part.
  (b) Assessments levied on businesses pursuant to this part shall be levied on the basis of the estimated benefit
  to the businesses within the property and business improvement district. The city council may classify
  businesses for purposes of determining the benefit to the businesses of the improvements and activities
  provided pursuant to this part.

36633. Time for contesting validity of assessment

The validity of an assessment levied under this part shall not be contested in an action or proceeding unless the action

36635. Request to modify management district plan

The owners’ association may, at any time, request that the city council modify the management district plan. Any
modification of the management district plan shall be made pursuant to this chapter.

36636. Modification of plan by resolution after public hearing; Adoption of resolution of intention

  (a) Upon the written request of the owners’ association, the city council may modify the management district
  plan after conducting one public hearing on the proposed modifications. The city council may modify the
  improvements and activities to be funded with the revenue derived from the levy of the assessments by
  adopting a resolution determining to make the modifications after holding a public hearing on the proposed
  modifications. If the modification includes the levy of a new or increased assessment, the city council shall
  comply with Section 36623. Notice of all other public hearings pursuant to this section shall comply with
  both of the following:
  (1) The resolution of intention shall be published in a newspaper of general circulation in the city
  once at least seven days before the public hearing.
  (2) A complete copy of the resolution of intention shall be mailed by first class mail, at least 10 days
  before the public hearing, to each business owner or property owner affected by the proposed
  modification.
  (b) The city council shall adopt a resolution of intention which states the proposed modification
  prior to the public hearing required by this section. The public hearing shall be held not more than
  90 days after the adoption of the resolution of intention.

36637. Reflection of modification in notices recorded and maps

Any subsequent modification of the resolution shall be reflected in subsequent notices and maps recorded pursuant to
Division 4.5 (commencing with Section 3100), in a manner consistent with the provisions of Section 36627.

36650. Report by owners’ association; Approval or modification by city council

  (a) The owners’ association shall cause to be prepared a report for each fiscal year, except the first year, for

  levying the assessments, and any changes in the classification of property, including any categories of
  business, if a classification is used.
  (b) The report shall be filed with the clerk and shall refer to the property and business improvement district

  all of the following information:
  (1) Any proposed changes in the boundaries of the property and business improvement district or in

  (2) The improvements, maintenance, and activities to be provided for that fiscal year.

  year.
  (4) The method and basis of levying the assessment in sufficient detail to allow each real property
  or business owner, as appropriate, to estimate the amount of the assessment to be levied against his
  or her property or business for that fiscal year.
  (5) The estimated amount of any surplus or deficit revenues to be carried over from a previous fiscal
  year.
  (6) The estimated amount of any contributions to be made from sources other than assessments
  levied pursuant to this part.

  contained in the report and approve it as modified. Any modification shall be made pursuant to Sections
  36635 and 36636.

  an authorized or executed contract to be paid from the revenues derived from the levy of assessments,
  including any commitment to pay principal and interest on any bonds issued on behalf of the district.

36651. Designation of owners’ association to provide improvements, maintenance, and activities

The management district plan may, but is not required to, state that an owners’ association will provide the
improvements, maintenance, and activities described in the management district plan. If the management district plan
designates an owners’ association, the city shall contract with the designated nonprofit corporation to provide services.

  CHAPTER 5. Renewal

36660. Renewal of district; Transfer or refund of remaining revenues; District term limit

  (a) Any district previously established whose term has expired, or will expire, may be renewed by following
  the procedures for establishment as provided in this chapter.
  (b) Upon renewal, any remaining revenues derived from the levy of assessments, or any revenues derived
  from the sale of assets acquired with the revenues, shall be transferred to the renewed district. If the renewed
  district includes additional parcels or businesses not included in the prior district, the remaining revenues
